source.edition: Textbook for Class XII Part I, Reprint 2026-27

chapter.name: Relations and Functions
chapter.blurb: This chapter studies types of relations in a set -- empty, universal, reflexive, symmetric, transitive and equivalence relations, together with the equivalence classes an equivalence relation creates. It then studies types of functions -- one-one, onto and bijective -- and closes with the composition of functions and invertible functions, where a function is invertible exactly when it is one-one and onto.

scope_in.item: Treat a relation from A to B as any subset of A x B (a relation in A as a subset of A x A), write (a, b) in R as a R b, and test whether a given ordered pair belongs to a relation given in set-builder form
Identify the empty relation (R = empty set) and the universal relation (R = A x A), both called trivial relations, including deciding which a set-builder condition gives

State the definitions of reflexive, symmetric and transitive relations and test a given relation (roster form, set-builder form on finite sets, N, Z, R, or a real-world set such as lines, triangles or people) for each property, giving a counterexample when a property fails

Prove that a relation is an equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric and transitive), e.g. congruence of triangles, 2 divides a - b in Z, same parity, same number of pages, similarity of triangles, parallel lines

Find equivalence classes [a] of an equivalence relation, and use the facts that classes are mutually disjoint, all elements of one class are related, and their union is the whole set (e.g. [0], [1], [2] for 3 divides a - b in Z)

Use the miscellaneous results: the intersection of two equivalence relations is an equivalence relation; R = {(a, b) : f(a) = f(b)} is an equivalence relation; the subset relation on P(X) is not an equivalence relation; count equivalence relations (or reflexive-transitive relations) on {1, 2, 3} containing given pairs
State and apply the definitions of one-one (injective) and many-one functions, proving one-one via f(x1) = f(x2) implies x1 = x2 and showing many-one with two distinct elements having the same image
State and apply the definitions of onto (surjective) functions (range = co-domain) and bijective functions, proving onto by finding a pre-image for an arbitrary element of the co-domain

Test standard functions recalled from Class XI for injectivity and surjectivity: x^2 and x^3 on N, Z, R, x^4, the greatest integer function, the modulus function, the signum function, 1/x on non-zero reals, piecewise odd/even functions on N, (x - 2)/(x - 3)
Use the finite-set property: for a finite set X, f : X -> X is one-one if and only if it is onto; this fails for infinite sets (f(x) = 2x on N)
Count one-one functions from {1, 2, 3} to itself (3! = 6) and onto functions from {1, 2, ..., n} to itself
Check whether a sum of functions (I_N + I_N, sin x + cos x on [0, pi/2]) keeps the one-one or onto property
Form the composition g o f, (g o f)(x) = g(f(x)), for functions on finite sets or on R, and show that g o f and f o g can differ

Define an invertible function (g o f = I_X and f o g = I_Y, inverse written f^(-1)), use the fact that f is invertible if and only if it is one-one and onto, and find the inverse of a simple function such as f(x) = 4x + 3 onto its range

concepts.name: Relations in a set; empty and universal relations
concepts.description: A relation from A to B as a subset of A x B, the notation a R b, and the two extreme (trivial) relations in a set: the empty relation and the universal relation.
concepts.idea: A relation R from a set A to a set B is any subset of A x B; a relation in a set A is a subset of A x A. If (a, b) is in R we write a R b.
concepts.rule: R is the empty relation if no element of A is related to any element of A (R = empty set); R is the universal relation if every element of A is related to every element of A (R = A x A). Both are called trivial relations.
concepts.example: In A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, R = {(a, b) : a - b = 10} is the empty relation, while R' = {(a, b) : |a - b| >= 0} is the universal relation A x A.

questions.q: A student says: 'In the set A of all students of a boys school, R = {(a, b) : a is brother of b} must be the empty relation, just like R = {(a, b) : a is sister of b}.' Is the student right? Explain.
questions.a: No. The sister relation is empty because no student of a boys school can be anyone's sister. But two students of a boys school can be brothers, so the brother relation need not be empty; it is empty only if no two students happen to be brothers, which the school being a boys school does not force.

s: States the claim is wrong because |a - b| >= 0 holds for every pair, including a = b

questions.q: For the set A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, write one condition in set-builder form that gives the empty relation in A and another that gives the universal relation in A. Justify each.
questions.a: For example, R = {(a, b) : a + b = 20} is empty, since a + b is at most 10 in A. S = {(a, b) : a + b <= 10} is universal, since every pair in A has a + b at most 10. (Any correctly justified pair of conditions earns full marks.)

Gives a condition that every pair in A x A satisfies

concepts.name: Reflexive, symmetric and transitive relations
concepts.description: Testing whether a relation in a set is reflexive, symmetric or transitive, and producing a counterexample when a property fails.
concepts.idea: Each of the three properties is a separate test on the pairs in R; a relation can have any combination of them.
concepts.rule: Reflexive: (a, a) is in R for every a in A. Symmetric: (a1, a2) in R implies (a2, a1) in R. Transitive: (a1, a2) in R and (a2, a3) in R imply (a1, a3) in R. One missing pair is enough to show a property fails.
concepts.example: In {1, 2, 3}, R = {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2), (2, 3)} is reflexive; it is not symmetric since (1, 2) is in R but (2, 1) is not; it is not transitive since (1, 2) and (2, 3) are in R but (1, 3) is not.

concepts.name: Equivalence relations and equivalence classes
concepts.description: Proving a relation is an equivalence relation, and finding the equivalence classes into which it divides the set.
concepts.idea: An equivalence relation sorts the elements of a set into mutually disjoint groups (equivalence classes) whose elements are all related to each other.
concepts.rule: R is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. The equivalence class [a] is the set of all elements related to a. Different classes have no common element and together make up the whole set.
concepts.example: R = {(a, b) : 2 divides a - b} in Z is an equivalence relation with two classes: [0], the even integers, and [1], the odd integers.

concepts.idea: A function is onto when nothing in the co-domain is left out: every element of Y is the image of something.
